## Why should you care? {.smaller data-menu-title="Motivation"}

**Every method in this deck answers one deceptively simple question: "did the intervention actually change anything?"**

- A hospital adopts a new treatment. Patients who received it look healthier — but were they already less sick when they were assigned?
- A tutoring program raises test scores. Were the volunteers already on an upward trajectory?
- A city installs cameras and crashes fall. Was it the cameras, or regression to the mean after a bad year?

::: {.block .alert data-title="The thread for the whole deck"}
Association tells you what happened together. Causal inference compares what happened with what **would have happened** had we acted differently. Graphs, estimators, and priors are all tools for making that comparison honest.
:::

[Keep one concrete example in mind as we go — the math is much easier when you have a story to attach it to.]{.small .muted}

## What you'll take away {data-menu-title="Goals"}

By the end of this deck you should be able to:

1. **Pose the question precisely** — name the treatment, the outcome, the population, and the estimand.
2. **Draw the story** — build a DAG and defend your adjustment set, including what *not* to adjust for.
3. **Choose an estimator** — know when regression, IPW, AIPW/DML, or a Bayesian model is the right tool.
4. **Interrogate the answer** — check overlap, run sensitivity analyses, and communicate uncertainty honestly.

::: {.block data-title="How to use this deck"}
Every simulation is live: drag a slider, press a button, rotate a graph, and watch the conclusion change. When a claim feels abstract, find the widget that lets you break it. Nothing here is meant to be taken on faith.
:::

# Foundations {#fundamentos .section-title background-color="#14213d"}

[From *what we observe* to *what we wish we knew*.]{.section-subtitle}

## Association versus causation

- An association is a property of $P(Y \mid T)$; a causal effect is a property of $P(Y \mid \operatorname{do}(T))$ or of potential outcomes.
- In general $P(y \mid t) \neq P(y \mid \operatorname{do}(t))$ when $T$ and $Y$ share common causes.
- Causal inference requires assumptions that cannot be checked from the observed data: the data alone do not identify the effect.

::: {.block .alert data-title="Guiding principle"}
No causal assumptions, no causal conclusions (Cartwright, Pearl).
:::

::: {.block data-title="In plain language"}
Correlation reports what was observed together; causation asks what would change if **you** stepped in and changed one thing. That "stepping in" is $\operatorname{do}(T)$.
:::

## The ladder of causation (Pearl)

| Level | Question | Object |
|:------|:---------|:-------|
| 1. Association | *What do we see?* | $P(y \mid x)$ |
| 2. Intervention | *What if I act?* | $P(y \mid \operatorname{do}(x))$ |
| 3. Counterfactual | *What would have happened?* | $P(y_x \mid x', y')$ |

Each level cannot be answered with information from the level below alone. This three-row table is the whole course in miniature.

## Simpson's paradox: kidney stones

|               | Small stones | Large stones | Total |
|:--------------|:----------------:|:---------------:|:-----:|
| Treatment A | 81/87 (93 %)  | 192/263 (73 %) | 273/350 (78 %) |
| Treatment B | 234/270 (87 %) | 55/80 (69 %)  | 289/350 (83 %) |

- Treatment A is better in **every** stratum, yet B looks better in the aggregate.
- Stone size is a confounder: it affects both treatment assignment and the outcome.
- The right decision depends on the DAG, not on the numbers alone.

## Simpson's paradox, live {.smaller}

:::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="55%"}
```{ojs}
viewof pA = Inputs.range([0, 1], {value: 263/350, step: 0.01, label: "Fraction of large stones in A"})
viewof pB = Inputs.range([0, 1], {value: 80/350, step: 0.01, label: "Fraction of large stones in B"})
```

```{ojs}
simpsonRows = {
  const r = {A: {peq: 81/87, gra: 192/263}, B: {peq: 234/270, gra: 55/80}};
  const tot = (k, p) => (1 - p) * r[k].peq + p * r[k].gra;
  return [
    {grupo: "Small", trat: "A", tasa: r.A.peq}, {grupo: "Small", trat: "B", tasa: r.B.peq},
    {grupo: "Large", trat: "A", tasa: r.A.gra}, {grupo: "Large", trat: "B", tasa: r.B.gra},
    {grupo: "Total", trat: "A", tasa: tot("A", pA)}, {grupo: "Total", trat: "B", tasa: tot("B", pB)}
  ];
}
Plot.plot({
  width: 620, height: 300, marginTop: 30,
  fx: {domain: ["Small", "Large", "Total"], label: null},
  x: {axis: null, domain: ["A", "B"]},
  y: {domain: [0, 1.08], label: "Success rate", tickFormat: "%", grid: true},
  color: {domain: ["A", "B"], range: ["#14213d", "#c8742b"], legend: true},
  marks: [
    Plot.barY(simpsonRows, {fx: "grupo", x: "trat", y: "tasa", fill: "trat"}),
    Plot.text(simpsonRows, {fx: "grupo", x: "trat", y: "tasa", text: d => (100 * d.tasa).toFixed(0) + "%", dy: -9, fontSize: 13})
  ]
})
```
:::
::: {.column width="45%"}
```{ojs}
{
  const a = simpsonRows[4].tasa, b = simpsonRows[5].tasa;
  return html`<div class="readout">
    Aggregate: A = <b>${(100*a).toFixed(1)}%</b>, B = <b>${(100*b).toFixed(1)}%</b><br>
    ${a < b ? "⚠️ <b>Paradox:</b> B 'wins' overall even though A wins in every stratum. A got the harder cases."
            : "✓ With similar case mixes, the aggregate favors A again."}
  </div>`;
}
```

Move the sliders: the rates **within** each stratum never change — only **who gets which cases** does. The aggregate mixes the treatment effect with the effect of severity.

```r
# Standardization (adjusting for the confounder)
w <- c(peq = 357, gra = 343) / 700   # P(stone size)
A <- c(81/87, 192/263); B <- c(234/270, 55/80)
sum(w * A) - sum(w * B)              # ≈ +0.05 in favor of A
```

# Potential Outcomes {#resultados-potenciales .section-title background-color="#14213d"}

[Every causal effect is a comparison of two worlds, only one of which we get to see.]{.section-subtitle}

## The Neyman–Rubin framework

::: {.block data-title="Definition 1"}
For each unit $i$ and binary treatment $T_i \in \{0,1\}$, the potential outcomes are $Y_i(1)$ and $Y_i(0)$. The observed outcome is
$$Y_i = T_i Y_i(1) + (1-T_i) Y_i(0).$$
:::

::: {.block data-title="The fundamental problem"}
For each $i$, only one of $Y_i(1), Y_i(0)$ is observed; the other is missing. The individual effect $\tau_i = Y_i(1) - Y_i(0)$ is not identifiable.
:::

## Causal estimands

$$
\begin{aligned}
\text{ATE} &= \mathbb{E}[Y(1) - Y(0)] \\
\text{ATT} &= \mathbb{E}[Y(1) - Y(0) \mid T = 1] \\
\text{ATC} &= \mathbb{E}[Y(1) - Y(0) \mid T = 0] \\
\text{CATE}(x) &= \mathbb{E}[Y(1) - Y(0) \mid X = x]
\end{aligned}
$$

- $\text{ATE} = \mathbb{P}(T=1)\,\text{ATT} + \mathbb{P}(T=0)\,\text{ATC}$.
- Also: quantile effects, risk-ratio effects, and odds-ratio effects.
- Choosing the *estimand* is a scientific decision that comes **before** choosing the *estimator*.

## The SUTVA assumption

::: {.block data-title="Definition 2 (SUTVA)"}
(i) *No interference*: $Y_i$ depends only on $T_i$, not on $T_j$ for $j \neq i$. (ii) *Single version*: there are no different versions of the treatment with different effects.
:::

- It fails with contagion, social networks, general-equilibrium or spillover effects.
- With interference the effect depends on the whole assignment vector $\mathbf{T}$, and direct and indirect estimands are needed.

## Assignment mechanism and selection bias

The naive difference in means decomposes as

$$
\mathbb{E}[Y \mid T=1] - \mathbb{E}[Y \mid T=0] = \underbrace{\text{ATT}}_{\text{effect}} + \underbrace{\mathbb{E}[Y(0) \mid T=1] - \mathbb{E}[Y(0) \mid T=0]}_{\text{selection bias}}.
$$

- The bias measures how different the groups would be **without** treatment.
- Randomization removes it because $T \perp\!\!\!\perp (Y(0), Y(1))$.

## Selection bias, live {.smaller}

:::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="58%"}
```{ojs}
viewof kSel = Inputs.range([-2, 2], {value: 1, step: 0.05, label: "Selection on X (k)"})
viewof aleat = Inputs.toggle({label: "Randomize T", value: false})
```

```{ojs}
selRes = {
  const rng = mulberry32(42), n = 20000;
  let s1 = 0, s0 = 0, n1 = 0, n0 = 0, y01 = 0, y00 = 0, att = 0;
  for (let i = 0; i < n; i++) {
    const x = randn(rng);
    const t = aleat ? (rng() < 0.5 ? 1 : 0) : (kSel * x + randn(rng) > 0 ? 1 : 0);
    const y0 = x + randn(rng), y1 = y0 + 1;   // true effect = 1
    if (t) { n1++; s1 += y1; y01 += y0; att += y1 - y0; } else { n0++; s0 += y0; y00 += y0; }
  }
  const naive = s1 / n1 - s0 / n0, sesgo = y01 / n1 - y00 / n0;
  return [
    {termino: "Naive difference", valor: naive},
    {termino: "ATT (effect)", valor: att / n1},
    {termino: "Selection bias", valor: sesgo}
  ];
}
Plot.plot({
  width: 640, height: 210, marginLeft: 150,
  marginBottom: 44, x: {domain: [-2, 3], label: "Value", grid: true, labelAnchor: "center", labelOffset: 36},
  y: {label: null, domain: selRes.map(d => d.termino)},
  marks: [
    Plot.barX(selRes, {y: "termino", x: "valor", fill: d => d.termino.startsWith("ATT") ? "#2e8b57" : d.termino.startsWith("Selection") ? "#c8742b" : "#14213d"}),
    Plot.text(selRes, {y: "termino", x: "valor", text: d => d.valor.toFixed(2), dx: 22}),
    Plot.ruleX([0])
  ]
})
```
:::
::: {.column width="42%"}
Model: $Y(0) = X + \varepsilon$, $Y(1) = Y(0) + 1$, and $T = \mathbb{1}\{kX + \eta > 0\}$.

- With $k > 0$, units with high $Y(0)$ get treated: the bias is **positive**.
- With $k < 0$, the bias flips sign.
- **Randomize** $T$ and the bias vanishes — the naive difference recovers the true effect.

```r
naive <- mean(Y[T == 1]) - mean(Y[T == 0])
sesgo <- mean(Y0[T == 1]) - mean(Y0[T == 0])
```
:::
::::

## Ignorability and positivity

::: {.block data-title="Definition 3 (Conditional ignorability)"}
$(Y(0), Y(1)) \perp\!\!\!\perp T \mid X$.
:::

::: {.block data-title="Definition 4 (Positivity / common support)"}
$0 < e(x) < 1$ for every $x$ with positive density, where $e(x) = \mathbb{P}(T = 1 \mid X = x)$.
:::

::: {.block .theorem data-title="Theorem 5 (Identifying the ATE)"}
Under SUTVA, ignorability, and positivity,
$$\text{ATE} = \mathbb{E}_X\big[\mathbb{E}(Y \mid T=1, X) - \mathbb{E}(Y \mid T=0, X)\big].$$
:::

## Why the identification theorem works

::: {.block data-title="Proof"}
By the law of iterated expectations,
$$
\begin{aligned}
\mathbb{E}[Y(1)] &= \mathbb{E}_X\big[\mathbb{E}(Y(1) \mid X)\big] \\
&= \mathbb{E}_X\big[\mathbb{E}(Y(1) \mid T=1, X)\big] && \text{(ignorability)} \\
&= \mathbb{E}_X\big[\mathbb{E}(Y \mid T=1, X)\big] && \text{(consistency).}
\end{aligned}
$$
Positivity guarantees that $\mathbb{E}(Y \mid T=1, X=x)$ is defined for every $x$. The same argument applies to $Y(0)$. $\square$
:::

## Randomized experiments

- Complete randomization: $T \perp\!\!\!\perp (Y(0), Y(1), X)$, so $\text{ATE} = \mathbb{E}[Y \mid T=1] - \mathbb{E}[Y \mid T=0]$.
- Neyman estimator: $\hat\tau = \bar Y_1 - \bar Y_0$, unbiased over the randomization distribution.
- Conservative variance: $\hat V = \dfrac{s_1^2}{n_1} + \dfrac{s_0^2}{n_0}$.
- Fisher's exact test: the sharp null $Y_i(1) = Y_i(0)$ for every $i$.
- Covariate adjustment (Lin, 2013) reduces variance without asymptotic bias.

## In code: analyzing an experiment

::: {.panel-tabset}
### R

```r
tau_hat <- mean(Y[T == 1]) - mean(Y[T == 0])                 # Neyman estimator
V_hat   <- var(Y[T == 1]) / sum(T) + var(Y[T == 0]) / sum(1 - T)
tau_hat + c(-1, 1) * qnorm(0.975) * sqrt(V_hat)

# Fisher's exact test approximated by permutation under the sharp null
perm <- replicate(10000, { Tp <- sample(T); mean(Y[Tp == 1]) - mean(Y[Tp == 0]) })
mean(abs(perm) >= abs(tau_hat))                               # p-value

# Lin (2013) adjustment: interactions with centered covariates + robust SEs
Xc  <- scale(X, scale = FALSE)
lin <- lm(Y ~ T * Xc)
coef(lin)["T"]          # use sandwich::vcovHC(lin, "HC2") for the standard error
```

### Python

```python
import numpy as np
rng = np.random.default_rng(1)
tau_hat = Y[T == 1].mean() - Y[T == 0].mean()
V_hat = Y[T == 1].var(ddof=1) / T.sum() + Y[T == 0].var(ddof=1) / (1 - T).sum()

perm = np.array([(lambda Tp: Y[Tp == 1].mean() - Y[Tp == 0].mean())(rng.permutation(T))
                 for _ in range(10_000)])
p_fisher = np.mean(np.abs(perm) >= abs(tau_hat))

import statsmodels.formula.api as smf      # Lin adjustment with HC2 standard errors
lin = smf.ols("Y ~ T * (X1_c + X2_c)", data=df).fit(cov_type="HC2")
```
:::

# Structural Causal Models {#modelos-causales-estructurales .section-title background-color="#14213d"}

[Draw the story first. The graph tells you what to measure — and what to leave alone.]{.section-subtitle}

## The structural causal model

::: {.block data-title="Definition 6 (SCM)"}
An SCM is $M = \langle U, V, F, P(U) \rangle$ with endogenous variables $V$, exogenous $U$, and functions $F = \{f_i\}$ such that $v_i = f_i(\mathrm{pa}_i, u_i)$.
:::

- The graph $G$ has an edge $V_j \to V_i$ if $V_j \in \mathrm{pa}_i$.
- Causal Markov condition: $P(v) = \prod_i P(v_i \mid \mathrm{pa}_i)$.
- An intervention $\operatorname{do}(T = t)$ replaces $f_T$ by the constant $t$ — *graph surgery*.

## Graph surgery in 3D {data-menu-title="DAG 3D"}

::: {.three-stage data-three="dag" data-prevent-swipe="" style="height: 560px"}
:::

[Press **do(T)** to erase arrows entering $T$; **adjust** puts a ring on the conditioned node. Orange pulses are open non-causal paths; green is the causal effect. Drag to rotate, click a node, and watch what opens and closes.]{.small .muted}

## Basic structures and d-separation


Chain, fork (confounder), and collider. A path is *blocked* by $Z$ if it contains a non-collider in $Z$, or a collider such that neither it nor any descendant is in $Z$. Conditioning on a collider does the opposite: it **opens** a path.

::: {.block .theorem data-title="Theorem 7"}
If $X$ and $Y$ are d-separated by $Z$ in $G$, then $X \perp\!\!\!\perp Y \mid Z$ in every distribution $P$ compatible with $G$.
:::

## d-separation, live {.smaller}

:::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="58%"}
```{ojs}
viewof estructura = Inputs.radio(["Chain A → B → C", "Fork A ← B → C", "Collider A → B ← C"], {value: "Collider A → B ← C"})
viewof condB = Inputs.toggle({label: "Condition on B", value: false})
```

```{ojs}
dsep = {
  const rng = mulberry32(5), n = 1200, rows = [];
  for (let i = 0; i < n; i++) {
    let A, B, C;
    if (estructura.startsWith("Chain")) { A = randn(rng); B = A + randn(rng); C = B + randn(rng); }
    else if (estructura.startsWith("Fork")) { B = randn(rng); A = B + randn(rng); C = B + randn(rng); }
    else { A = randn(rng); C = randn(rng); B = A + C + 0.5 * randn(rng); }
    rows.push({A, B, C});
  }
  const sB = Math.sqrt(rows.reduce((s, r) => s + r.B * r.B, 0) / n);
  rows.forEach(r => r.sel = Math.abs(r.B) < 0.2 * sB);
  return rows;
}
Plot.plot({
  width: 640, height: 330, grid: true,
  marginBottom: 44, x: {domain: [-4.5, 4.5], label: "A", labelAnchor: "center", labelOffset: 36}, y: {domain: [-5, 5], label: "C"},
  marks: [
    Plot.dot(dsep, {x: "A", y: "C", r: 2, fill: condB ? "#b9c1d0" : "#14213d", fillOpacity: condB ? 0.4 : 0.5}),
    condB ? Plot.dot(dsep.filter(d => d.sel), {x: "A", y: "C", r: 3, fill: "#c8742b"}) : null,
    Plot.linearRegressionY(condB ? dsep.filter(d => d.sel) : dsep, {x: "A", y: "C", stroke: condB ? "#c8742b" : "#14213d", strokeWidth: 3, ci: 0})
  ]
})
```
:::
::: {.column width="42%"}
```{ojs}
{
  const r = rows => {
    const n = rows.length, ma = d3.mean(rows, d => d.A), mc = d3.mean(rows, d => d.C);
    let sac = 0, saa = 0, scc = 0;
    for (const d of rows) { sac += (d.A - ma) * (d.C - mc); saa += (d.A - ma) ** 2; scc += (d.C - mc) ** 2; }
    return sac / Math.sqrt(saa * scc);
  };
  const all = r(dsep), sel = r(dsep.filter(d => d.sel));
  const col = estructura.startsWith("Coll");
  return html`<div class="readout">
    Marginal corr(A, C): <b>${all.toFixed(2)}</b><br>
    corr(A, C | B ≈ 0): <b>${sel.toFixed(2)}</b><br><br>
    ${col ? "In a <b>collider</b>, A and C are independent — but conditioning on B <b>opens</b> the path and creates a spurious correlation."
          : "In a chain or fork, A and C are associated, but conditioning on B <b>blocks</b> the path."}
  </div>`;
}
```

```r
library(dagitty)
g <- dagitty("dag { A -> B <- C }")
dseparated(g, "A", "C", list())   # TRUE
dseparated(g, "A", "C", "B")      # FALSE
```
:::

## Structural biases

- [Confounding]{.hl}: an open backdoor path $T \leftarrow X \rightarrow Y$.
- [Collider bias]{.hl}: conditioning on $C$ in $T \to C \leftarrow Y$ opens a spurious path.
- [Overadjustment]{.hl}: conditioning on a mediator $M$ in $T \to M \to Y$ blocks part of the effect.
- [M-bias]{.hl}: conditioning on a pre-treatment collider of two unobserved causes.

The rule "adjust for everything measured before treatment" is **not** generally correct — the graph decides.

## The backdoor criterion

::: {.block data-title="Definition 8 (Backdoor)"}
$Z$ satisfies the backdoor criterion for $(T, Y)$ if (i) no node in $Z$ is a descendant of $T$ and (ii) $Z$ blocks every path between $T$ and $Y$ that contains an arrow into $T$.
:::

::: {.block .theorem data-title="Theorem 9"}
If $Z$ satisfies the criterion, then
$$P(y \mid \operatorname{do}(t)) = \sum_z P(y \mid t, z)\, P(z).$$
:::

This is equivalent to conditional ignorability given $Z$, and it justifies regression, IPW, and matching.

## The frontdoor criterion

```{=html}
<svg viewBox="0 0 600 170" width="560" height="160" style="display:block;margin:0 auto;font-family:'Source Sans 3',sans-serif;font-style:italic;font-size:24px">
  <defs><marker id="ah2" viewBox="0 0 10 10" refX="9" refY="5" markerWidth="7" markerHeight="7" orient="auto"><path d="M0,0 L10,5 L0,10 z" fill="#14213d"/></marker></defs>
  <g fill="none" stroke="#14213d" stroke-width="2.2">
    <circle cx="300" cy="35" r="24" stroke-dasharray="5 4"/>
    <circle cx="100" cy="135" r="24"/><circle cx="300" cy="135" r="24"/><circle cx="500" cy="135" r="24"/>
    <line x1="124" y1="135" x2="272" y2="135" marker-end="url(#ah2)"/><line x1="324" y1="135" x2="472" y2="135" marker-end="url(#ah2)"/>
    <line x1="280" y1="48" x2="124" y2="122" stroke-dasharray="6 5" marker-end="url(#ah2)"/><line x1="320" y1="48" x2="476" y2="122" stroke-dasharray="6 5" marker-end="url(#ah2)"/>
  </g>
  <g fill="#14213d" text-anchor="middle" dominant-baseline="central">
    <text x="300" y="35">U</text><text x="100" y="135">T</text><text x="300" y="135">M</text><text x="500" y="135">Y</text>
  </g>
</svg>
```

If $M$ intercepts every directed path from $T$ to $Y$, there is no backdoor $T \leftarrow \cdot \rightarrow M$, and $T$ blocks the paths from $M \to Y$:
$$P(y \mid \operatorname{do}(t)) = \sum_m P(m \mid t) \sum_{t'} P(y \mid m, t')\, P(t').$$

It identifies the effect even when the confounder $U$ is unobserved — a genuinely remarkable result.

## In code: identification from the DAG

::: {.panel-tabset}
### R · dagitty

```r
library(dagitty)
g <- dagitty("dag {
  X -> T ; X -> Y
  U -> T ; U -> Y
  T -> M -> Y
  U [latent]
}")
adjustmentSets(g, exposure = "T", outcome = "Y")  # no set: U blocks the backdoor
adjustmentSets(g, exposure = "M", outcome = "Y")  # { T }: frontdoor, stage 2
impliedConditionalIndependencies(g)               # testable implications
```

### Python · DoWhy

```python
from dowhy import CausalModel

model = CausalModel(
    data=df, treatment="T", outcome="Y",
    graph="digraph { X -> T; X -> Y; U -> T; U -> Y; T -> M; M -> Y; }",
)  # U is not in df: treated as unobserved
estimand = model.identify_effect()        # finds the frontdoor estimand
print(estimand)
est = model.estimate_effect(estimand, method_name="frontdoor.two_stage_regression")
```
:::

## do-calculus {.smaller}

Let $G_{\overline{X}}$ be the graph with arrows into $X$ removed and $G_{\underline{Z}}$ the graph with arrows out of $Z$ removed.

1. **Insertion/deletion of observations**: if $(Y \perp\!\!\!\perp Z \mid X, W)_{G_{\overline{X}}}$, then $P(y \mid \operatorname{do}(x), z, w) = P(y \mid \operatorname{do}(x), w)$.
2. **Action/observation**: if $(Y \perp\!\!\!\perp Z \mid X, W)_{G_{\overline{X}\underline{Z}}}$, then $P(y \mid \operatorname{do}(x), \operatorname{do}(z), w) = P(y \mid \operatorname{do}(x), z, w)$.
3. **Insertion/deletion of actions**: if $(Y \perp\!\!\!\perp Z \mid X, W)_{G_{\overline{X}\,\overline{Z(W)}}}$, then $P(y \mid \operatorname{do}(x), \operatorname{do}(z), w) = P(y \mid \operatorname{do}(x), w)$.

::: {.block .theorem data-title="Theorem 10 (Completeness, Shpitser–Pearl; Huang–Valtorta)"}
A causal effect is identifiable from $P(v)$ and $G$ **if and only if** it can be derived using these three rules.
:::

## Counterfactuals in an SCM

To evaluate $P(Y_t \mid T = t', Y = y')$, follow three steps:

1. **Abduction**: update $P(U)$ with the evidence $\{T = t', Y = y'\}$ to obtain $P(U \mid t', y')$.
2. **Action**: modify the model with $\operatorname{do}(T = t)$.
3. **Prediction**: compute the distribution of $Y$ in the modified model using $P(U \mid t', y')$.

Counterfactuals are identifiable only with extra assumptions about $f$ (e.g. monotonicity); treatment effects and probabilities of necessity and sufficiency can still be bounded.

# Classical Estimation {#estimación-clásica .section-title background-color="#14213d"}

[Four tools, one goal: recover a comparison that nature did not hand us.]{.section-subtitle}

## Regression and the Frisch–Waugh–Lovell theorem

Model $Y = \alpha + \tau T + X^\top \beta + \varepsilon$.

::: {.block .theorem data-title="Theorem 11 (FWL)"}
$\hat\tau$ equals the slope from regressing $\tilde Y = Y - \hat Y(X)$ on $\tilde T = T - \hat T(X)$.
:::

- $\hat\tau$ estimates the ATE if $\mathbb{E}[Y(t) \mid X]$ is linear in $X$ and the effect is homogeneous; with heterogeneity it estimates a weighted average, with weights proportional to $\mathbb{V}(T \mid X)$.
- Include $T \times X$ interactions (imputation estimator / g-computation) to let the effect vary.

```r
ry <- resid(lm(Y ~ X1 + X2, d)); rt <- resid(lm(T ~ X1 + X2, d))
all.equal(unname(coef(lm(ry ~ rt))[2]),                     # TRUE: FWL
          unname(coef(lm(Y ~ T + X1 + X2, d))["T"]))
fit <- lm(Y ~ T * (X1 + X2), d)                           # g-computation
mean(predict(fit, transform(d, T = 1)) - predict(fit, transform(d, T = 0)))
```

## The propensity score

::: {.block .theorem data-title="Theorem 12 (Rosenbaum–Rubin, 1983)"}
If $(Y(0), Y(1)) \perp\!\!\!\perp T \mid X$ and $0 < e(X) < 1$, then $(Y(0), Y(1)) \perp\!\!\!\perp T \mid e(X)$.
:::

::: {.block data-title="Proof"}
$\mathbb{P}(T=1 \mid Y(0), Y(1), e(X)) = \mathbb{E}\big[\mathbb{E}(T \mid Y(0), Y(1), X) \mid Y(0), Y(1), e(X)\big] = \mathbb{E}[e(X) \mid Y(0), Y(1), e(X)] = e(X)$. Since this no longer depends on $(Y(0), Y(1))$, ignorability holds. $\square$
:::

The balancing score collapses many covariates into one number: $X \perp\!\!\!\perp T \mid e(X)$. That is why it is so useful.

## The propensity surface $e(x)$ in 3D {data-menu-title="Propensity 3D"}

::: {.three-stage data-three="propensity" data-prevent-swipe="" style="height: 560px"}
:::

[Raise **confounding γ**: the surface turns into a step, the groups stop overlapping, and a handful of IPW weights $1/\hat e$ dominate. This is positivity in action — and the moment estimation becomes fragile.]{.small .muted}

## Inverse probability weighting (IPW)

$$
\hat\tau_{\text{IPW}} = \frac{1}{n} \sum_{i=1}^n \left[ \frac{T_i Y_i}{\hat e(X_i)} - \frac{(1-T_i) Y_i}{1 - \hat e(X_i)} \right]
$$

::: {.block data-title="Unbiasedness with known e"}
$\mathbb{E}\Big[\frac{TY}{e(X)}\Big] = \mathbb{E}\Big[\frac{T\,Y(1)}{e(X)}\Big] = \mathbb{E}\Big[\frac{\mathbb{E}(T \mid X, Y(1))}{e(X)} Y(1)\Big] = \mathbb{E}[Y(1)]$. $\square$
:::

- Variance explodes when $e(X)$ is near 0 or 1; use stabilization (Hájek) or trimming.
- Weights for the ATT: $T + (1-T)\,\hat e / (1 - \hat e)$.

## Matching and stratification

- **Nearest neighbor** on $e(X)$ or Mahalanobis distance, with or without replacement.
- **Abadie–Imbens**: impute the counterfactual from the $M$ nearest neighbors, with a regression-adjusted bias correction.
- **Stratification**: five subclasses on $e(X)$ remove about $90\%$ of the bias (Cochran).
- **Balance**: check standardized mean differences $|\text{SMD}| < 0.1$ after matching.
- Score matching is not $\sqrt{n}$-consistent with the usual variance formula: use Abadie–Imbens standard errors or an appropriate bootstrap.

```r
library(MatchIt); library(marginaleffects)
m  <- matchit(T ~ X1 + X2, data = d, method = "nearest", distance = "glm", caliper = 0.1)
summary(m)                                        # |SMD| before and after
md <- match.data(m)
fit <- lm(Y ~ T * (X1 + X2), data = md, weights = weights)
avg_comparisons(fit, variables = "T", vcov = ~subclass,
                newdata = subset(md, T == 1), wts = "weights")   # ATT
```

## The doubly robust estimator (AIPW) {.smaller}

$$
\hat\psi_i = \hat\mu_1(X_i) - \hat\mu_0(X_i) + \frac{T_i (Y_i - \hat\mu_1(X_i))}{\hat e(X_i)} - \frac{(1-T_i)(Y_i - \hat\mu_0(X_i))}{1 - \hat e(X_i)}, \qquad \hat\tau = \tfrac{1}{n} \textstyle\sum_i \hat\psi_i
$$

::: {.block .theorem data-title="Theorem 13 (Double robustness)"}
$\hat\tau$ is consistent if **either** $\hat e$ **or** $\hat\mu_t$ is consistent — two chances to get it right.
:::

::: {.block data-title="Why it works"}
If $\hat e = e$: $\mathbb{E}[T(Y - \hat\mu_1)/e] = \mathbb{E}[Y(1) - \hat\mu_1(X)]$, which cancels the first term. If $\hat\mu_1 = \mu_1$: $\mathbb{E}[T(Y - \mu_1)/\hat e] = \mathbb{E}\big[\tfrac{T}{\hat e}(\mathbb{E}(Y \mid X, T=1) - \mu_1)\big] = 0$. $\square$
:::

## In code: IPW and AIPW

::: {.panel-tabset}
### R

```r
ps  <- fitted(glm(T ~ X1 + X2, family = binomial, data = d))
ipw <- mean(T * Y / ps) - mean((1 - T) * Y / (1 - ps))            # Horvitz–Thompson
w1 <- T / ps; w0 <- (1 - T) / (1 - ps)
hajek <- sum(w1 * Y) / sum(w1) - sum(w0 * Y) / sum(w0)             # stabilized (Hájek)

mu1 <- predict(lm(Y ~ X1 + X2, data = d, subset = T == 1), d)
mu0 <- predict(lm(Y ~ X1 + X2, data = d, subset = T == 0), d)
psi <- mu1 - mu0 + T * (Y - mu1) / ps - (1 - T) * (Y - mu0) / (1 - ps)
c(aipw = mean(psi), se = sd(psi) / sqrt(nrow(d)))                  # SE from the influence function
```

### Python

```python
import numpy as np
from sklearn.linear_model import LogisticRegression, LinearRegression

e = LogisticRegression(penalty=None).fit(X, T).predict_proba(X)[:, 1]
mu1 = LinearRegression().fit(X[T == 1], Y[T == 1]).predict(X)
mu0 = LinearRegression().fit(X[T == 0], Y[T == 0]).predict(X)

ipw = np.mean(T * Y / e) - np.mean((1 - T) * Y / (1 - e))
psi = mu1 - mu0 + T * (Y - mu1) / e - (1 - T) * (Y - mu0) / (1 - e)
aipw, se = psi.mean(), psi.std(ddof=1) / np.sqrt(len(psi))
```
:::

## Lab: which estimator survives? {.smaller}

:::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="40%"}
```{ojs}
viewof labGamma = Inputs.range([0, 2.5], {value: 1.2, step: 0.1, label: "Confounding γ"})
viewof labN = Inputs.range([200, 2000], {value: 500, step: 100, label: "n per replicate"})
viewof labBadE = Inputs.toggle({label: "ê(X) misspecified (omits X₂)", value: false})
viewof labBadMu = Inputs.toggle({label: "μ̂(X) misspecified (omits X₂)", value: false})
```

[60 Monte Carlo replicates. Truth: $\tau = 2$. Model: $T \sim \text{Bern}(\text{expit}(\gamma(0.7X_1 + 0.9X_2)))$, $Y = 1 + 2T + X_1 + 1.5X_2 + \varepsilon$. Break one or both nuisance models and watch what survives.]{.tiny}

```{ojs}
html`<div class="readout" style="font-size:0.95em">${labTable.map(d => `<div>${d.metodo}: bias <b>${d.sesgo.toFixed(2)}</b>, SD ${d.de.toFixed(2)}</div>`).join("")}
<div style="margin-top:6px">${labBadE && labBadMu ? "Both models are wrong: even AIPW cannot save us." : (labBadE || labBadMu) ? "One model is wrong, but <b>AIPW</b> stays centered at 2 — that is double robustness." : "All models correct: every adjustment works, and AIPW has the smallest spread."}</div></div>`
```
:::
::: {.column width="60%"}
```{ojs}
labRes = {
  const rng = mulberry32(99), n = labND, out = [];
  const dot = (a, b) => { let t = 0; for (let k = 0; k < a.length; k++) t += a[k] * b[k]; return t; };
  for (let r = 0; r < 60; r++) {
    const T = new Float64Array(n), Y = new Float64Array(n), rowsE = [], rows1 = [], rows0 = [], rowsMu = [];
    for (let i = 0; i < n; i++) {
      const x1 = randn(rng), x2 = randn(rng);
      const t = rng() < expit(labGammaD * (0.7 * x1 + 0.9 * x2)) ? 1 : 0;
      T[i] = t; Y[i] = 1 + 2 * t + x1 + 1.5 * x2 + randn(rng);
      // precompute design rows once per replicate
      rowsE.push(labBadE ? [1, x1] : [1, x1, x2]);
      rows1.push(labBadMu ? [1, 1, x1] : [1, 1, x1, x2]);
      rows0.push(labBadMu ? [1, 0, x1] : [1, 0, x1, x2]);
      rowsMu.push(t ? rows1[i] : rows0[i]);
    }
    const bE = logitFit(rowsE, T), bMu = olsFit(rowsMu, Y);
    let m1 = 0, m0 = 0, n1 = 0, sw1 = 0, sw0 = 0, sy1 = 0, sy0 = 0, aipw = 0;
    for (let i = 0; i < n; i++) {
      const e = Math.min(0.995, Math.max(0.005, expit(dot(bE, rowsE[i]))));
      const mu1 = dot(bMu, rows1[i]), mu0 = dot(bMu, rows0[i]);
      if (T[i]) { m1 += Y[i]; n1++; sw1 += 1 / e; sy1 += Y[i] / e; }
      else { m0 += Y[i]; sw0 += 1 / (1 - e); sy0 += Y[i] / (1 - e); }
      aipw += mu1 - mu0 + T[i] * (Y[i] - mu1) / e - (1 - T[i]) * (Y[i] - mu0) / (1 - e);
    }
    out.push({metodo: "Naive", est: m1 / n1 - m0 / (n - n1)});
    out.push({metodo: "Regression", est: bMu[1]});
    out.push({metodo: "IPW (Hajek)", est: sy1 / sw1 - sy0 / sw0});
    out.push({metodo: "AIPW", est: aipw / n});
  }
  return out;
}
labTable = d3.groups(labRes, d => d.metodo).map(([metodo, v]) => ({
  metodo, sesgo: d3.mean(v, d => d.est) - 2, de: d3.deviation(v, d => d.est)
}))
Plot.plot({
  width: 700, height: 360, marginLeft: 100,
  marginBottom: 44, x: {domain: [0.5, 5.5], label: "Effect estimate (60 replicates)", grid: true, labelAnchor: "center", labelOffset: 36},
  y: {domain: ["Naive", "Regression", "IPW (Hajek)", "AIPW"], label: null},
  color: {domain: ["Naive", "Regression", "IPW (Hajek)", "AIPW"], range: ["#9aa3b5", "#14213d", "#c8742b", "#2e8b57"]},
  marks: [
    Plot.ruleX([2], {stroke: "#2e8b57", strokeWidth: 2, strokeDasharray: "6 4"}),
    Plot.boxX(labRes, {x: "est", y: "metodo", fill: "metodo", fillOpacity: 0.35, stroke: "metodo"}),
  ]
})
```
:::
::::

## Machine learning and double debiasing {.smaller}

- Efficient influence function of the ATE: $\psi = \mu_1 - \mu_0 + \frac{T(Y - \mu_1)}{e} - \frac{(1-T)(Y - \mu_0)}{1-e} - \tau$; its variance is the semiparametric efficiency bound.
- **DML** (Chernozhukov et al., 2018): estimate $\mu_t$ and $e$ with ML plus *cross-fitting*. Neyman orthogonality gives $\sqrt{n}$-consistency when nuisance errors multiply to $o_p(n^{-1/2})$.
- **TMLE** (van der Laan): a targeted updating step that respects the efficiency bound.
- **Causal forests** (Wager–Athey): estimate $\text{CATE}(x)$ with asymptotic inference.

::: {.panel-tabset}
### R · DoubleML

```r
library(DoubleML); library(mlr3); library(mlr3learners)
dml_data <- DoubleMLData$new(d, y_col = "Y", d_cols = "T", x_cols = c("X1", "X2"))
irm <- DoubleMLIRM$new(dml_data, ml_g = lrn("regr.ranger"),
                       ml_m = lrn("classif.ranger"), n_folds = 5)
irm$fit(); irm$summary()
```

### R · grf

```r
library(grf)
cf <- causal_forest(X = as.matrix(d[, c("X1", "X2")]), Y = d$Y, W = d$T)
average_treatment_effect(cf, target.sample = "all")   # AIPW with forests
tau_x <- predict(cf)$predictions                       # CATE(x_i)
```

### Python · DoubleML

```python
import doubleml as dml
from sklearn.ensemble import RandomForestRegressor, RandomForestClassifier
data = dml.DoubleMLData(df, y_col="Y", d_cols="T", x_cols=["X1", "X2"])
irm = dml.DoubleMLIRM(data, ml_g=RandomForestRegressor(), ml_m=RandomForestClassifier(), n_folds=5)
irm.fit(); print(irm.summary)
```
:::

## Difference in differences

$$
\tau_{\text{DiD}} = \big(\mathbb{E}[Y_1 \mid T=1] - \mathbb{E}[Y_0 \mid T=1]\big) - \big(\mathbb{E}[Y_1 \mid T=0] - \mathbb{E}[Y_0 \mid T=0]\big)
$$

::: {.block .theorem data-title="Theorem 14"}
Under parallel trends, $\mathbb{E}[Y_1(0) - Y_0(0) \mid T=1] = \mathbb{E}[Y_1(0) - Y_0(0) \mid T=0]$, and with no anticipation, $\tau_{\text{DiD}} = \text{ATT}$.
:::

- With staggered adoption, two-way fixed effects can assign negative weights; use Callaway–Sant'Anna, Sun–Abraham, or de Chaisemartin–D'Haultfœuille.
- Check pre-trends with event-study plots — the single most convincing diagnostic in DiD.

```r
library(did)
out <- att_gt(yname = "y", tname = "anio", idname = "id", gname = "primer_trat",
              data = panel, control_group = "notyettreated")
ggdid(aggte(out, type = "dynamic"))   # event study: pre-trends ≈ 0
```

## Instrumental variables

An instrument $Z$ needs: relevance $\operatorname{Cov}(Z, T) \neq 0$; independence $Z \perp\!\!\!\perp (Y(t), T(z))$; exclusion $Y(t, z) = Y(t)$; monotonicity $T(1) \geq T(0)$.

::: {.block .theorem data-title="Theorem 15 (LATE, Imbens–Angrist)"}
$$\frac{\mathbb{E}[Y \mid Z=1] - \mathbb{E}[Y \mid Z=0]}{\mathbb{E}[T \mid Z=1] - \mathbb{E}[T \mid Z=0]} = \mathbb{E}[Y(1) - Y(0) \mid T(1) > T(0)].$$
:::

- It estimates the effect for *compliers*, not the ATE. Know who you are talking about.
- Weak instruments: bias toward OLS and non-standard inference (first-stage $F$, Anderson–Rubin).

```r
library(fixest)
iv <- feols(Y ~ X1 | T ~ Z, data = d)      # MC2E
summary(iv); fitstat(iv, ~ ivf + ivwald)    # first-stage F
```

## Regression discontinuity and synthetic control

**RDD** with assignment variable $X$ and cutoff $c$:
$$\tau_{\text{RD}} = \lim_{x \downarrow c} \mathbb{E}[Y \mid X = x] - \lim_{x \uparrow c} \mathbb{E}[Y \mid X = x],$$
identified if $\mathbb{E}[Y(t) \mid X = x]$ is continuous at $c$. Estimate by local regression with an optimal bandwidth (Imbens–Kalyanaraman; Calonico–Cattaneo–Titiunik), and test for density manipulation (McCrary).

**Synthetic control**: weights $w_j \geq 0$, $\sum w_j = 1$ minimizing $\|X_1 - X_0 w\|$; the counterfactual is $\sum_j w_j Y_{jt}$. Inference comes from placebo tests.

## RDD live: choosing the bandwidth {.smaller}

:::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="62%"}
```{ojs}
viewof rdH = Inputs.range([0.05, 1], {value: 0.3, step: 0.01, label: "Bandwidth h"})
```

```{ojs}
rdData = {
  const rng = mulberry32(17), out = [];
  for (let i = 0; i < 600; i++) {
    const x = 2 * rng() - 1;
    out.push({x, y: 0.4 + 0.9 * x - 0.9 * x * x + 0.5 * (x >= 0) + 0.25 * randn(rng)});
  }
  return out;
}
rdFit = {
  const side = (s) => {
    let sw = 0, sx = 0, sy = 0, sxx = 0, sxy = 0, k = 0;
    for (const d of rdData) {
      if ((s > 0) !== (d.x >= 0) || Math.abs(d.x) >= rdH) continue;
      const w = 1 - Math.abs(d.x) / rdH; k++;
      sw += w; sx += w * d.x; sy += w * d.y; sxx += w * d.x * d.x; sxy += w * d.x * d.y;
    }
    const b = (sw * sxy - sx * sy) / (sw * sxx - sx * sx), a = (sy - b * sx) / sw;
    return {a, b, k};
  };
  const L = side(-1), R = side(1);
  return {L, R, tau: R.a - L.a};
}
Plot.plot({
  width: 700, height: 340, grid: true,
  marginBottom: 44, x: {domain: [-1, 1], label: "Assignment variable X (cutoff c = 0)", labelAnchor: "center", labelOffset: 36}, y: {label: "Y"},
  marks: [
    Plot.rect([{x1: -rdH, x2: rdH}], {x1: "x1", x2: "x2", fill: "#c8742b", fillOpacity: 0.08}),
    Plot.dot(rdData, {x: "x", y: "y", r: 2, fill: d => Math.abs(d.x) < rdH ? "#14213d" : "#c3c9d6"}),
    Plot.line([[-rdH, rdFit.L.a - rdFit.L.b * rdH], [0, rdFit.L.a]], {stroke: "#c8742b", strokeWidth: 3}),
    Plot.line([[0, rdFit.R.a], [rdH, rdFit.R.a + rdFit.R.b * rdH]], {stroke: "#c8742b", strokeWidth: 3}),
    Plot.ruleX([0], {strokeDasharray: "4 3"})
  ]
})
```
:::
::: {.column width="38%"}
```{ojs}
html`<div class="readout">τ̂<sub>RD</sub> = <b>${rdFit.tau.toFixed(3)}</b> (truth: 0.5)<br>
Observations used: ${rdFit.L.k + rdFit.R.k}<br><br>
${rdH > 0.6 ? "Large h: more data, but curvature biases the local fit." : rdH < 0.12 ? "Small h: little bias, but high variance." : "A reasonable bias–variance trade-off."}</div>`
```

Local linear regression with a triangular kernel on each side of the cutoff. `rdrobust` picks $h$ optimally and corrects the bias:

```r
library(rdrobust); library(rddensity)
summary(rdrobust(y, x, c = 0))   # optimal h + robust CI
rdplot(y, x, c = 0)
summary(rddensity(x, c = 0))     # manipulation test
```
:::
::::

## Sensitivity to unmeasured confounding {.smaller}

- **Rosenbaum bounds**: a parameter $\Gamma$ such that $\frac{1}{\Gamma} \leq \frac{e(x)/(1 - e(x))}{e(x')/(1 - e(x'))} \leq \Gamma$ for matched units.
- **E-value** (VanderWeele–Ding): $E = \text{RR} + \sqrt{\text{RR}(\text{RR} - 1)}$, the minimum association an unmeasured confounder would need with both $T$ and $Y$ to explain away the effect.
- **Cinelli–Hazlett**: $R^2_{Y \sim U \mid T, X}$ and $R^2_{T \sim U \mid X}$ as sensitivity contours.
- **Manski bounds**: partial identification without ignorability assumptions.

:::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="55%"}
```{ojs}
viewof rrObs = Inputs.range([1.05, 5], {value: 2, step: 0.05, label: "Observed RR"})
```
```{ojs}
{
  const E = rrObs + Math.sqrt(rrObs * (rrObs - 1));
  const curve = d3.range(rrObs + 0.02, 12, 0.02).map(u => ({u, v: rrObs * (u - 1) / (u - rrObs)})).filter(d => d.v <= 12);
  return Plot.plot({
    width: 560, height: 250, grid: true,
    marginBottom: 44, x: {domain: [1, 12], label: "Confounder–outcome RR", labelAnchor: "center", labelOffset: 36}, y: {domain: [1, 12], label: "Confounder–treatment RR"},
    marks: [
      Plot.areaY(curve, {x: "u", y1: "v", y2: 12, fill: "#c8742b", fillOpacity: 0.15}),
      Plot.line(curve, {x: "u", y: "v", stroke: "#c8742b", strokeWidth: 2.5}),
      Plot.dot([{E}], {x: "E", y: "E", r: 6, fill: "#14213d"}),
      Plot.text([{E}], {x: "E", y: "E", text: d => `E = ${d.E.toFixed(2)}`, dx: 40, dy: -10, fontWeight: 600})
    ]
  });
}
```
:::
::: {.column width="45%"}
[The shaded region contains confounders strong enough to explain away the entire observed effect.]{.small}

```r
library(EValue); library(sensemakr)
evalues.RR(est = 2.0, lo = 1.5, hi = 2.7)
s <- sensemakr(lm(Y ~ T + X1 + X2, d),
      treatment = "T",
      benchmark_covariates = "X1", kd = 1:3)
plot(s)   # Cinelli–Hazlett contours
```

::::

## Classical inference

- **Asymptotic normality**: $\sqrt{n}(\hat\tau - \tau) \to N(0, V)$, with $V = \mathbb{V}(\psi)$ for efficient estimators.
- **Sandwich variance** (Huber–White) for misspecified models.
- **Bootstrap**: valid for smooth IPW/AIPW; not valid for nearest-neighbor matching with replacement.
- **Confidence intervals** cover $\tau$ in $100(1-\alpha)\%$ of repeated samples. They do **not** give a probability for $\tau$ given your data.
- **Randomization inference** (Fisher) for small samples.

## What does "95% confidence" mean? {.smaller}

:::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="62%"}
```{ojs}
viewof ciDraw = Inputs.button("Draw 50 new samples")
viewof ciLevel = Inputs.radio([0.80, 0.90, 0.95, 0.99], {value: 0.95, label: "Level", format: d => `${100 * d}%`})
```

```{ojs}
ciRows = {
  const rng = mulberry32(1000 + ciDraw), n = 25, z = qnorm(1 - (1 - ciLevel) / 2), rows = [];
  for (let k = 0; k < 50; k++) {
    let s = 0; for (let i = 0; i < n; i++) s += 2 + randn(rng);
    const m = s / n, h = z / Math.sqrt(n);
    rows.push({k, lo: m - h, hi: m + h, m, cubre: m - h <= 2 && 2 <= m + h});
  }
  return rows;
}
Plot.plot({
  width: 700, height: 380, marginBottom: 44, x: {domain: [1, 3], label: "τ", grid: true, labelAnchor: "center", labelOffset: 36}, y: {axis: null},
  color: {domain: [true, false], range: ["#14213d", "#d1495b"]},
  marks: [
    Plot.ruleX([2], {stroke: "#2e8b57", strokeWidth: 2}),
    Plot.link(ciRows, {x1: "lo", x2: "hi", y1: "k", y2: "k", stroke: "cubre", strokeWidth: 2}),
    Plot.dot(ciRows, {x: "m", y: "k", r: 2.5, fill: "cubre"})
  ]
})
```
:::
::: {.column width="38%"}
```{ojs}
html`<div class="readout">Intervals covering τ = 2: <b>${ciRows.filter(d => d.cubre).length} of 50</b><br>(nominal: ${100 * ciLevel}%)</div>`
```

The probability belongs to the **procedure** over repeated sampling. Any single interval either covers $\tau$ or it does not; the failures are red.

The question "how probable is $\tau > 0$ given *these* data?" is Bayesian →
:::
::::

# Bayesian Causal Inference {#inferencia-causal-bayesiana .section-title background-color="#14213d"}

[Treat the missing counterfactual as uncertainty you can actually quantify.]{.section-subtitle}

## Rubin's Bayesian perspective

- Missing potential outcomes $Y_{\text{mis}}$ are treated as unknown quantities with a posterior distribution.
- Model: $p(Y(0), Y(1), X, T) = p(Y(0), Y(1), X \mid \theta)\, p(T \mid Y(0), Y(1), X, \phi)$, with $\theta$ and $\phi$ independent a priori.
- An estimand $\tau = \tau(Y(0), Y(1))$ inherits a posterior distribution:
$$p(\tau \mid D) = \iint p(\tau \mid Y_{\text{obs}}, Y_{\text{mis}}, \theta)\, p(Y_{\text{mis}} \mid D, \theta)\, p(\theta \mid D)\, dY_{\text{mis}}\, d\theta.$$

## Ignorability of the assignment mechanism

::: {.block .theorem data-title="Theorem 16 (Rubin, 1978)"}
If $p(T \mid Y(0), Y(1), X, \phi) = p(T \mid X, \phi)$ and $\theta \perp\!\!\!\perp \phi$ a priori, then the posterior for $\theta$ does not depend on $\phi$ or on the assignment model:
$$p(\theta \mid X, Y_{\text{obs}}, T) \propto p(\theta) \int p(Y_{\text{obs}}, Y_{\text{mis}}, X \mid \theta)\, dY_{\text{mis}}.$$
:::

- When assignment is ignorable, you can infer $\theta$ without modeling $T$ at all.
- Non-ignorability requires modeling $(Y, T)$ jointly with informative priors.

## The Bayesian outcome model

$$Y_i \mid T_i, X_i, \theta \sim N(\mu_{T_i}(X_i), \sigma^2), \qquad \mu_t(x) = \alpha_t + x^\top \beta_t.$$

Priors: $\beta \sim N(\mu_0, \Sigma_0)$, $\sigma^2 \sim \text{Inv-}\chi^2$. With known $\sigma^2$:

$$\beta \mid D \sim N(m, S), \quad S = \Big(\frac{X^\top X}{\sigma^2} + \Sigma_0^{-1}\Big)^{-1}, \quad m = S\Big(\frac{X^\top y}{\sigma^2} + \Sigma_0^{-1}\mu_0\Big).$$

The posterior mean is a precision-weighted average of the prior and the least-squares estimate: shrinkage toward $\mu_0$.

## The conjugate posterior in 3D {data-menu-title="Posterior 3D"}

::: {.three-stage data-three="bayes" data-prevent-swipe="" style="height: 560px"}
:::

[Model $y = \alpha + \tau T + \varepsilon$ with a prior $N(0, s_0^2 I)$. With **little data or a tight prior**, the posterior stays near $\mu_0 = 0$; with **more data**, it concentrates around OLS and the truth.]{.small .muted}

## Bayesian g-computation

For each posterior draw $\theta^{(s)} \sim p(\theta \mid D)$:

1. Predict $\tilde Y_i(1)$ and $\tilde Y_i(0)$ for every unit from the posterior predictive distribution (or the conditional mean).
2. Compute $\tau^{(s)} = \frac{1}{n} \sum_i \big[\tilde Y_i(1) - \tilde Y_i(0)\big]$ (sample ATE), or average over $p(x)$ (population ATE).

The collection $\{\tau^{(s)}\}$ approximates $p(\tau \mid D)$. Summarize it with the mean, median, 95% credible interval, HPD region, and $\mathbb{P}(\tau > 0 \mid D)$.

::: {.block .alert data-title="Key distinction"}
The sample ATE includes uncertainty about $Y_{\text{mis}}$; the population ATE also includes uncertainty about the distribution of $X$.
:::

## In code: Bayesian g-computation

::: {.panel-tabset}
### R · brms

```r
library(brms)
fit <- brm(Y ~ T * (X1 + X2), data = d, family = gaussian(),
           prior = prior(normal(0, 5), class = "b"), chains = 4, cores = 4)

mu1 <- posterior_epred(fit, newdata = transform(d, T = 1))   # S x n
mu0 <- posterior_epred(fit, newdata = transform(d, T = 0))
tau <- rowMeans(mu1 - mu0)                                   # draws from p(ATE | D)
c(mean = mean(tau), quantile(tau, c(.025, .975)), P_pos = mean(tau > 0))
```

### Python · PyMC

```python
import numpy as np, pymc as pm

with pm.Model():
    a = pm.Normal("a", 0, 5); tau = pm.Normal("tau", 0, 5)
    b = pm.Normal("b", 0, 5, shape=2); g = pm.Normal("g", 0, 5, shape=2)   # T × X
    s = pm.HalfNormal("s", 2)
    mu = a + tau * T + X @ b + T * (X @ g)
    pm.Normal("y", mu, s, observed=Y)
    idata = pm.sample()

post = idata.posterior
ate = post["tau"].values + post["g"].values @ X.mean(axis=0)   # sample ATE (conditional mean)
print(ate.mean(), np.quantile(ate, [0.025, 0.975]), (ate > 0).mean())
```

### R base (conjugate)

```r
X  <- model.matrix(~ T * (X1 + X2), d);  S0 <- diag(25, ncol(X))
s2 <- summary(lm(Y ~ T * (X1 + X2), d))$sigma^2
S  <- solve(crossprod(X) / s2 + solve(S0));  m <- S %*% crossprod(X, Y) / s2
B  <- matrix(rnorm(4000 * ncol(X)), 4000) %*% chol(S) + rep(1, 4000) %o% drop(m)
D  <- colMeans(model.matrix(~ T * (X1 + X2), transform(d, T = 1)) -
               model.matrix(~ T * (X1 + X2), transform(d, T = 0)))
tau <- drop(B %*% D);  quantile(tau, c(.025, .5, .975))
```
:::

[Complete, verified script in base R: [`code/inferencia_causal.R`](code/inferencia_causal.R).]{.code-note}

## Priors and regularization

- **Weakly informative priors**: $N(0, 5^2)$ on standardized coefficients.
- **Shrinkage priors** for heterogeneity: horseshoe, Laplace, regularized horseshoe.
- **Hierarchical priors**: $\tau_g \sim N(\tau, \sigma_\tau^2)$ for partial pooling across subgroups.
- **Bias priors**: one bias parameter per unmeasured confounder, propagating that uncertainty into $\tau$.
- Always run a prior sensitivity analysis and prior predictive checks.

```r
prior(horseshoe(df = 1, par_ratio = 0.1), class = "b")       # brms: shrinkage
bf(Y ~ T + X1 + X2 + (1 + T | grupo))                          # partial pooling of tau_g
brm(..., sample_prior = "only")                                # prior predictive
```

## Nonparametric models: BART

$$f(t, x) = \sum_{j=1}^m g(t, x; \mathcal{T}_j, \mathcal{M}_j), \qquad Y = f(T, X) + \varepsilon, \ \varepsilon \sim N(0, \sigma^2)$$

- A regularization prior on tree depth and leaf size keeps every tree weak.
- $\tau(x) = f(1, x) - f(0, x)$, with a posterior over $\text{CATE}(x)$; Hill (2011).
- Including the propensity score as a covariate helps under strong confounding (Hahn, Murray, and Carvalho: *BCF*).
- Uncertainty stays honest when extrapolating outside common support: intervals widen.

```r
library(bartCause)
fit <- bartc(response = Y, treatment = T, confounders = X1 + X2, data = d,
             estimand = "ate", method.trt = "glm")   # ê(x) as a covariate
summary(fit);  cate <- fitted(fit, type = "icate")  # posterior of CATE(x_i)
```

## Propensity score and feedback

- A Bayesian estimate of $e(x)$ propagates its uncertainty into $\tau$.
- **Feedback problem**: $Y$ contaminates the posterior for $e$ in a joint model; use a *cut* or a two-stage model.
- Even though the likelihood does not depend on $e$ under ignorability, including $\hat e(X)$ as a covariate protects against outcome misspecification (Robins–Ritov).
- A Bayesian IPW estimator uses a *Bayesian bootstrap* (Dirichlet weights).

```r
bb <- replicate(1000, {
  g  <- rexp(nrow(d))                   # unnormalized Dirichlet(1, ..., 1) weights
  e  <- fitted(glm(T ~ X1 + X2, quasibinomial, d, weights = g))  # refit ê(X)
  a1 <- g * d$T / e; a0 <- g * (1 - d$T) / (1 - e)
  sum(a1 * d$Y) / sum(a1) - sum(a0 * d$Y) / sum(a0)
})
quantile(bb, c(.025, .975))             # includes uncertainty about ê(X)
```

## Bayesian IV and DiD

- **Bayesian IV**: joint model $T = \gamma_0 + \gamma_1 Z + \nu$, $Y = \alpha + \tau T + \varepsilon$ with $(\nu, \varepsilon) \sim N(0, \Sigma)$; posterior over $\tau$ and the error correlation. Priors soften weak-instrument problems.
- **Bayesian DiD / structural time series**: counterfactual $\tilde Y_t(0)$ from a state-space model (CausalImpact, Brodersen et al.).
- **Bayesian synthetic control**: weights with a Dirichlet prior.
- **Heterogeneous effects**: hierarchical models across subgroups.

```r
library(CausalImpact)
impact <- CausalImpact(serie, pre.period = c(1, 70), post.period = c(71, 100))
summary(impact); plot(impact)
```

## Diagnostics and model checking

- **MCMC convergence**: $\hat R < 1.01$, effective sample size $> 400$ per parameter, no NUTS divergences.
- **Posterior predictive checks**: compare $y^{\text{rep}} \sim p(y \mid D)$ with the observed $y$.
- **Cross-validation**: PSIS-LOO to compare specifications of $\mu_t$.
- **Sensitivity**: vary the prior, the outcome specification, and the covariate set.
- **Common support**: inspect overlap in $\hat e(x)$ across groups.

```r
library(posterior)
summarise_draws(as_draws_df(fit), "rhat", "ess_bulk", "ess_tail")
pp_check(fit, ndraws = 50)                           # posterior predictive check
loo_compare(loo(fit), loo(fit_no_interactions))   # PSIS-LOO
```

## Decision-making with the causal posterior

- $\mathbb{P}(\tau > 0 \mid D)$ and $\mathbb{P}(\tau > \delta \mid D)$ for a practically meaningful threshold $\delta$.
- **ROPE**: region of practical equivalence $[-\delta, \delta]$; compare posterior mass inside and outside.
- **Decision theory**: choose the action $a$ maximizing $\int U(a, \tau)\, p(\tau \mid D)\, d\tau$.
- **Value of information**: expected cost of remaining uncertainty.
- Bayesian **stopping rules** for adaptive trials, with no penalty for looking at the data.

## Prior × likelihood → decision {.smaller}

:::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="36%"}
```{ojs}
viewof bm0 = Inputs.range([-2, 2], {value: 0, step: 0.05, label: "Prior mean"})
viewof bs0 = Inputs.range([0.1, 3], {value: 1, step: 0.05, label: "Prior SD"})
viewof bhat = Inputs.range([-1, 3], {value: 0.6, step: 0.05, label: "τ̂ (data)"})
viewof bse = Inputs.range([0.05, 1.5], {value: 0.4, step: 0.05, label: "Standard error"})
viewof bdelta = Inputs.range([0, 1], {value: 0.2, step: 0.05, label: "Threshold δ (ROPE)"})
```

```{ojs}
bpost = {
  const p = 1 / bs0 ** 2 + 1 / bse ** 2, m = (bm0 / bs0 ** 2 + bhat / bse ** 2) / p, s = Math.sqrt(1 / p);
  return {m, s, pPos: 1 - pnorm(-m / s), pDelta: 1 - pnorm((bdelta - m) / s),
          pRope: pnorm((bdelta - m) / s) - pnorm((-bdelta - m) / s),
          lo: m - 1.96 * s, hi: m + 1.96 * s};
}
html`<div class="readout">
  Posterior: N(<b>${bpost.m.toFixed(2)}</b>, ${bpost.s.toFixed(2)}²)<br>
  95% credible interval: [${bpost.lo.toFixed(2)}, ${bpost.hi.toFixed(2)}]<br>
  P(τ > 0 | D) = <b>${bpost.pPos.toFixed(3)}</b><br>
  P(τ > δ | D) = <b>${bpost.pDelta.toFixed(3)}</b><br>
  P(|τ| < δ | D) = <b>${bpost.pRope.toFixed(3)}</b> (ROPE)
</div>`
```
:::
::: {.column width="64%"}
```{ojs}
{
  const xs = d3.range(-3, 4.001, 0.02);
  const dens = (m, s) => xs.map(x => ({x, y: dnorm((x - m) / s) / s}));
  const curves = [
    ...dens(bm0, bs0).map(d => ({...d, curva: "Prior"})),
    ...dens(bhat, bse).map(d => ({...d, curva: "Likelihood"})),

    marks: [

      Plot.areaY(post.filter(d => d.x >= bdelta), {x: "x", y: "y", fill: "#c8742b", fillOpacity: 0.3}),
      Plot.line(curves, {x: "x", y: "y", stroke: "curva", strokeWidth: d => 2}),

      Plot.ruleY([0])
    ]
  });
}
```

# Comparison and Takeaways {#comparación-y-cierre .section-title background-color="#14213d"}

[Method is a tool; the question is the boss.]{.section-subtitle}

## Classical versus Bayesian

| Aspect | Classical | Bayesian |
|:--------|:--------|:----------|
| Parameter | Fixed and unknown | Random variable |
| Counterfactual | Missing data, not modeled | Imputed from the predictive |
| Uncertainty | Sampling distribution | Posterior distribution |
| Interval | Confidence | Credible |
| Prior information | Not formal | Explicit priors |
| Small samples | Asymptotic results | Exact inference given the model |
| Robustness | Double robustness, efficiency | Depends on model and prior |

## Identification versus estimation

- Identification is a *population* question: can the estimand be written as a functional of $P(\text{observable})$?
- Estimation and inference are *sample* questions: how do we estimate that functional and quantify uncertainty?
- Priors and regularization control variance; they [do not]{.hl} fix a lack of identification.
- In partially identified settings the posterior never collapses to a point: it converges to the identified set, and the prior keeps mattering asymptotically.

## A workflow you can reuse

1. Write down the question, the estimand, and the target population.
2. Draw the DAG and justify the adjustment set using substantive knowledge.
3. Check positivity and overlap — look at the data, not just the theory.
4. Estimate with several methods (regression, IPW, AIPW/DML, Bayesian).
5. Examine balance, diagnostics, and specification.
6. Quantify sensitivity to unmeasured confounding.
7. Report effects with uncertainty **and** explicit assumptions.

## Conclusions

- Causality is defined with potential outcomes or SCMs; identification rests on assumptions.
- The right adjustment comes from the graph, not from throwing in every covariate.
- AIPW/DML give efficiency and double robustness; Bayesian methods deliver full posterior distributions and handle uncertainty naturally.
- Sensitivity analysis is part of the analysis, not an appendix.

The R script for this edition ([`code/inferencia_causal.R`](code/inferencia_causal.R)) implements OLS/FWL, g-computation, IPW, AIPW, matching, Bayesian g-computation, and a Bayesian bootstrap on simulated data. Run it yourself — learning by breaking things is the fastest route to intuition.

```{ojs}
//| output: false
labGammaD = debounce(viewof labGamma)
labND = debounce(viewof labN)
mulberry32 = (seed) => {
  let a = seed >>> 0;
  return () => {
    a |= 0; a = (a + 0x6d2b79f5) | 0;
    let t = Math.imul(a ^ (a >>> 15), 1 | a);
    t = (t + Math.imul(t ^ (t >>> 7), 61 | t)) ^ t;
    return ((t ^ (t >>> 14)) >>> 0) / 4294967296;
  };
}
randn = (rng) => { let u = 0; while (u === 0) u = rng(); return Math.sqrt(-2 * Math.log(u)) * Math.cos(2 * Math.PI * rng()); }
expit = (x) => 1 / (1 + Math.exp(-x))
dnorm = (z) => Math.exp(-0.5 * z * z) / Math.sqrt(2 * Math.PI)
pnorm = (z) => {
  // Abramowitz–Stegun 26.2.17
  const t = 1 / (1 + 0.2316419 * Math.abs(z));
  const p = dnorm(z) * t * (0.31938153 + t * (-0.356563782 + t * (1.781477937 + t * (-1.821255978 + t * 1.330274429))));
  return z >= 0 ? 1 - p : p;
}
qnorm = (p) => {
  let lo = -10, hi = 10;
  for (let i = 0; i < 80; i++) { const mid = (lo + hi) / 2; if (pnorm(mid) < p) lo = mid; else hi = mid; }
  return (lo + hi) / 2;
}
solveLin = (A, b) => {
  const n = b.length, M = A.map((r, i) => [...r, b[i]]);
  for (let c = 0; c < n; c++) {
    let p = c; for (let r = c + 1; r < n; r++) if (Math.abs(M[r][c]) > Math.abs(M[p][c])) p = r;
    [M[c], M[p]] = [M[p], M[c]];
    for (let r = 0; r < n; r++) if (r !== c) { const f = M[r][c] / M[c][c]; for (let k = c; k <= n; k++) M[r][k] -= f * M[c][k]; }
  }
  return M.map((r, i) => r[n] / r[i]);
}
olsFit = (X, y, w) => {
  const p = X[0].length, A = Array.from({length: p}, () => new Array(p).fill(0)), b = new Array(p).fill(0);
  X.forEach((x, i) => { const wi = w ? w[i] : 1; for (let j = 0; j < p; j++) { b[j] += wi * x[j] * y[i]; for (let k = 0; k < p; k++) A[j][k] += wi * x[j] * x[k]; } });
  return solveLin(A, b);
}
logitFit = (X, y) => {
  let beta = new Array(X[0].length).fill(0);
  for (let it = 0; it < 10; it++) {
    const w = [], z = [];
    X.forEach((x, i) => {
      const eta = x.reduce((s, v, k) => s + v * beta[k], 0), mu = Math.min(1 - 1e-6, Math.max(1e-6, expit(eta))), wi = mu * (1 - mu);
      w.push(wi); z.push(eta + (y[i] - mu) / wi);
    });
    const next = olsFit(X, z, w);
    const delta = next.reduce((m, v, k) => Math.max(m, Math.abs(v - beta[k])), 0);
    beta = next;
    if (delta < 1e-6) break;
  }
  return beta;
}
// Emit an input's value at most once every `delay` ms (avoids recomputing on every slider pixel)
debounce = (input, delay = 250) => Generators.observe(notify => {
  let timer = null, value;
  const inputted = () => {
    if (timer !== null) return;
    notify(value = input.value);
    timer = setTimeout(delayed, delay);
  };
  const delayed = () => { timer = null; if (value !== input.value) notify(value = input.value); };
  input.addEventListener("input", inputted);
  inputted();
  return () => input.removeEventListener("input", inputted);
})
```
